title: Brother of man who died after being hit by a police Taser says he doesn't blame police
article: The brother of an Edmonton man who died after being zapped by a Taser multiple times by police says he holds no resentment towards the responding officers.
Marcel Moisan, 49, died Monday after being hit with a city police Taser at his northeast Edmonton home at 12004 58 St. But his brother, Randy Moisan, says police were only doing their jobs.

"My brother had a knife, he wouldn't drop the knife. They (used a Taser on) him, and he wouldn't go down so they (used a Taser on) him again. Then they went to go handcuff him, and he woke up. The knife was beside him and he grabbed the knife again and put it to his throat," said Moisan, 53.

"Do I blame the police? No. They had to do what they had to do. They were trying to save his life. They took a chance at saving him by (using a Taser on) him, but unfortunately it did not go that way."
Those who knew Moisan agree that he had some sort of breakdown Monday, resulting in an 11:30 p.m. 911 call to police from a rental home where his wife and 14-year-old son also live.
Contrary to reports stating Marcel's wife was home at the time of the incident, Randy says his brother was home alone at the time with his son.
He says his brother was awake for four straight days prior to Monday's incident, and that his brother suffered from mental illness.

"He (Marcel) was mentally ill. He was chemically dependant, and unfortunately it took a hold of him and he never sought the help he needed," said Moisan, adding his brother only began taking up drugs a few months ago.

"He doesn't even smoke cigarettes. He wouldn't even smoke a joint when he was a teenager. And the thing is, the place where he got this stuff is two doors down. I know it's everywhere - no matter where you go, you can't hide from it."
But ultimately, Moisan remembers his brother most as a "jokester, who was full of life" and as a "competitive guy" who loved sports.
"I don't want people to think my brother was a wacked-out, drug-addict, freak," said Moisan.
"He was a hard worker, he was generous, he had a heart of gold. Even though I'm the older brother, as he got older he felt he had to protect me, and he always did that. I'm going to miss him."
Moisan was to appear in court Monday after Oct. 30 offences that led to charges of assault, two counts of obstructing a peace officer, and assaulting a peace officer causing bodily harm.

Moisan had last been in trouble with the law in March of 1998, when was handed six months probation and had to enter a peace bond after being charged with assault and threatening injury or damage. In 1997, he was given 12 months probation for possession of a dangerous weapon (a bat).
The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) is probing the death.

ASIRT's probe will focus on the circumstances surrounding the police contact with the victim to determine whether their conduct caused the death and, if so, whether that conduct constitutes a criminal offence. Cause of death will be determined by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner following an autopsy.
This is the second in-custody Edmonton city police death since October and the third in 2015. The other two ASIRT cases have still not concluded.
A viewing and funeral for Moisan will take place on Tuesday, Dec.15 at the Evergreen Memorial & Funeral Chapels in Edmonton.
- With files from Nicole Bergot
